## Goals

After this lecture, you should be able to:

- execute the Euclidean algorithm efficiently;
- justify why replacing $(a,b)$ by $(b,r)$ preserves the common divisors;
- recover Bézout coefficients by back-substitution;
- decide when a residue class has a multiplicative inverse.

## Greatest common divisors

::: {#def-gcd}
## Greatest common divisor

For integers $a$ and $b$, not both zero, the **greatest common divisor** $\gcd(a,b)$ is the unique positive integer $d$ such that

1. $d\mid a$ and $d\mid b$;
2. every common divisor of $a$ and $b$ divides $d$.
:::

The second condition is stronger and more useful than merely saying that $d$ is the largest common divisor.

## The reduction step

Suppose the division algorithm gives

$$a=bq+r.$$

A number divides both $a$ and $b$ exactly when it divides both $b$ and $r=a-bq$. Therefore

$$\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,r).$$

Repeating this replacement strictly decreases the positive remainder, so the process must stop.

::: {#thm-euclidean-algorithm}
## Euclidean algorithm

Let $a\ge b>0$. Repeatedly divide with remainder:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a&=bq_1+r_1,\\
b&=r_1q_2+r_2,\\
&\ \vdots\\
r_{k-2}&=r_{k-1}q_k+r_k,\\
r_{k-1}&=r_kq_{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then the last nonzero remainder is $\gcd(a,b)$.
:::

## Worked example

Compute $\gcd(252,198)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
252&=198\cdot1+54,\\
198&=54\cdot3+36,\\
54&=36\cdot1+18,\\
36&=18\cdot2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\gcd(252,198)=18$.

The calculation contains more information. Reading upward,

$$
\begin{aligned}
18&=54-36\\
  &=54-(198-3\cdot54)\\
  &=4\cdot54-198\\
  &=4(252-198)-198\\
  &=4\cdot252-5\cdot198.
\end{aligned}
$$

We have expressed the gcd as an integer linear combination.

::: {#thm-bezout}
## Bézout's identity

For integers $a$ and $b$, not both zero, there exist integers $x$ and $y$ such that

$$ax+by=\gcd(a,b).$$
:::

::: {.proof}
The Euclidean algorithm terminates at the gcd. Each remainder is an integer linear combination of the two preceding numbers. Back-substitution therefore expresses the final nonzero remainder as an integer linear combination of the original inputs.
:::

## Consequences

::: {#cor-linear-diophantine}
## Linear Diophantine criterion

The equation

$$ax+by=c$$

has an integer solution if and only if $\gcd(a,b)\mid c$.
:::

For modular arithmetic, Bézout's identity gives an especially useful test.

::: {#cor-inverse-criterion}
## Inverse criterion

The congruence

$$ax\equiv1\pmod n$$

has a solution if and only if $\gcd(a,n)=1$.
:::

::: {.example}
**Example.** To invert $17$ modulo $43$, run the Euclidean algorithm:

$$43=2\cdot17+9,\quad 17=1\cdot9+8,\quad 9=1\cdot8+1.$$

Back-substitution gives

$$1=2\cdot43-5\cdot17.$$

Therefore $-5$ is an inverse of $17$ modulo $43$, and the least nonnegative inverse is $38$.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
**Exercise 1.** Compute $\gcd(414,662)$ and express it in the form $414x+662y$.
:::

::: {.exercise}
**Exercise 2.** Determine all integers $c$ for which $84x+126y=c$ has an integer solution.
:::

::: {.exercise}
**Exercise 3.** Find the inverse of $37$ modulo $101$ without trial and error.

<details class="hint"><summary>Check after solving</summary>
Multiply your proposed inverse by $37$ and reduce modulo $101$.
</details>
:::

::: {.exercise}
**Exercise 4.** Prove that $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(a,a+b)$ for all integers $a,b$, not both zero.
:::

## Summary

The Euclidean algorithm is simultaneously a computational procedure and a proof. It identifies the gcd, certifies it through a Bézout identity, and solves the inverse problem in modular arithmetic.
